paras: The Pleasant View posse shooting was a gunfight on the night of August 7-8, 1900, near Pleasant View, Amherst County, Virginia, between a special constable's posse of eight white men and the Black family of Paul Smith, whom they came to arrest at home. All eight posse members were reported wounded, none fatally, and the Smiths surrendered on the understanding that they would be protected from a mob and not lynched. Virginia papers followed the case to forty-one indictments, while the Richmond Planet praised the family's armed defense of their home against a "mob."

According to Deputy Sheriff A. D. Beard, the quarrel began when health officials quarantined a Black church because of smallpox. The family blamed Constable William Martin, a neighbor who had posted the notice, and on Tuesday evening the young Smiths and the Martins had a row in which both sides fired without hitting anyone. A Lynchburg dispatch said one of the Smith sons had torn down the notice and then had "a difficulty" with Martin, who swore out a warrant, while the first Amherst report said a Black man had threatened to burn Martin's dwelling.

Because Martin was a party to the quarrel, Justice R. C. Wilsher appointed T. J. Carter special constable to make the arrests, and Carter summoned seven men. The posse reached Paul Smith's house about one o'clock on Wednesday morning, and in Beard's account the Smiths, called out two or three times, answered by raising their windows and firing.

About fifty shots were exchanged; the Lynchburg dispatch said two sons did the family's firing from behind a chicken coop with a breechloader and an old pistol. Every man in the posse was hit, three seriously; the Norfolk Virginian-Pilot added that one of the Smiths was slightly wounded and that the family had four guns and a pistol.

By morning a crowd had gathered at the house, reinforcing the officers. Paul Smith then came out and gave himself up, asking protection, and the family surrendered on the understanding that they would not be lynched and would have a fair trial.

At the preliminary hearing before Justice Wilsher, white and Black onlookers stood on opposite sides of the road, and Beard found "excitement running high." Beard took four prisoners to Amherst Courthouse that evening, and the Smiths were sent on to the grand jury. On August 9 Paul Smith and his sons Creed, Walter and Wilson were moved to the Lynchburg jail for safekeeping; they retained A. E. Strode as counsel.

By August 17 the wounded men were said to be doing well and the Smiths were to be taken to Amherst Courthouse for trial. On August 24 a Lynchburg dispatch reported forty-one indictments against five defendants, Paul Smith, his sons Wilson, Ellis and Creed, and Nelson Smith; no report of a verdict appears in the coverage.

The first white report, an Amherst dispatch to the Richmond Times, said eight white men had been shot "by a negro mob," and a Lynchburg dispatch to the same paper said the affair "almost rivals the recent events in New Orleans." Later Times dispatches gave the family's side, noted that white sentiment was "somewhat divided," and printed Beard's description of Paul Smith as a "thrifty negro, who has accumulated some property."

The Lynchburg dispatch of August 9 ran as "Smith Family Shot to Kill" in the Washington Weekly Post and as "Wounded by Negroes" in the Lexington Gazette, and the Virginian-Pilot set out both versions of who fired first.

The Richmond Planet, on August 18, called the posse "the mob" and its wounded "would-be lynchers," and questioned a special constable's authority to take a man from his home at night. It wrote that Smith "did just as any other American citizen with a spark of manhood would have done" and urged that citizens of the South "fire on mobs first and ask questions afterwards."

The deputy sheriff and the posse's side said the family fired from the windows when called out, while the Smiths said the posse fired first and that they took the men for "white cappers." The first Lynchburg report named Constable Martin as leader and counted five wounded; later reports gave eight, the Pilot headline and the Planet nine.

reader.title: Pleasant View posse shooting
bases: A special constable's posse of eight, serving warrants from a justice of the peace, went to a Black family's house at night and exchanged about fifty shots with them; no one was killed, and the family surrendered on a promise that they would not be lynched (A5, A7, A8).

Separate Amherst and Lynchburg dispatches (A1, A5, A7, A8), plus the Richmond Planet (A12), agree that a posse went to Paul Smith's house, that shots were exchanged, that the posse was wounded and that the Smiths were jailed; who fired first is disputed (A4, A5, A8).

accounts.label: Deputy sheriff's statement
accounts.gist: Carter called the Smiths out two or three times; they made no reply but raised their windows and fired into the posse, wounding all eight. The quarrel grew from the church quarantine and a Tuesday row with the Martins.

accounts.label: Smith family's statement
accounts.gist: The Martins attacked them in the afternoon and the posse opened fire on the house without a word that night; they did not know of a warrant and thought the men were white cappers.

accounts.label: First Lynchburg report
accounts.gist: One son of Paul Smith, wanted on Constable Martin's warrant for threats, met the posse of eight with a breechloading shotgun and wounded five.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet editorial
accounts.gist: A mob led by a self-styled special constable came at night without lawful authority; Smith, his two sons and nephew rightly defended their home and later surrendered on assurance of protection.

framing.detail: The first Richmond Times report said eight white men were shot 'by a negro mob' and a Lynchburg dispatch likened it to New Orleans, but later Times dispatches printed the Smiths' version, the deputy sheriff's praise of Paul Smith and a note that white sentiment was divided.
The Virginian-Pilot ('Nine Men Wounded') gave both versions of who fired first and stressed that 'wiser counsels prevailed' at the tense hearing.
The Lynchburg dispatch ran as 'Smith Family Shot to Kill / Believed Officers White Caps' in the Washington Weekly Post and as 'Wounded by Negroes' in the Lexington Gazette.
The Richmond Planet called the posse 'the mob' and 'would-be lynchers', said Smith 'deserves credit and his sons should wear laurels', and urged Black men to arm.
